Newsgroups:   alt.books.kurt-Vonnegut
Subject:      Vonnegut and the Unabomber
From:         jmswart@rs6000.cmp.ilstu.edu (Jason Michael Swarts)
Date:         1996/07/23

    After re-reading the "Industrialized Society and It's Future"
again, I happened upon this passage that struck me as being something
similar to what Vonnegut says (or at least implies) about the human
condition.

     I don't intend for the post to seem like an official sanctioning
of bombing or murder.  Instead, I would like to demonstrate that this
manifesto can be looked at in a larger academic, revolutionary
capacity rather than simply as a justification for terrorism.

    In "The Nature of Freedom" (Part 12 of the Manifesto) the
Unabomber writes that

     Freedom means being in control (either as an individual
     or as a member of a SMALL gropu) of the life-and-death
     issues  of one's existence . . . Freedom means having
     power; not the power to control other people but the power
     to control the circumstances of one's own life"

Granted, Vonnegut's characters are not much for demonstrating that
they are in charge of the circumstances of their own existence, but in
that existential angst is what seems to be some sort of implied
resistance.  A small revolutionary movement that is happening at the
character level, right beneath the surface of the story.  It is one
thing to accept that we are not in control of the circumstances of our
own existences (let alone anybody elses) and slip into a sort of
nihilistic view of life but Vonnegut's characters seem to have this
spark of revolutionary energy in them.  That keeps them from becoming
totally detestable.

     At a lecture given by Vonnegut that I attended, he told us that
we all needed to form our own gangs.  A couple of people laughed at
this suggestion (for which Vonnegut snapped angrily at them) and so he
went on to clarify this position.  Vonnegut said that in an
increasingly alienating family and social existence, the need to get
back to collectivities and extended families reveals itself as one of
the most promising ways of re-cultivating some sort of purpose in an
individual's life.  In a way, I see the Unabomber arguing the same
thing.  I don't really have any textual evidence right before me, but
_Dead Eye Dick_, _Jailbird_, _Breakfast of Champions_, and Kilgore
Trout come readily to mind....

any thoughts?
